detrimental

/det-ruh-MEN-tul/ — stress on MEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Detrimental describes something that causes harm or damage, especially over time.

Leaving the bike out in the rain all winter was detrimental to its gears.

Example

The coach warned that skipping practice would be detrimental to their performance in the tournament.

Detriment (harm, damage) + -al = characteristic of harm. Skipping practice causes harm to their athletic development and readiness. The base word 'detriment' and adjective 'detrimental' travel together: something works to a team's detriment (noun) / something is detrimental to a team (adjective).

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

injurious: Injurious means causing injury — harm, often physical or lasting, done to a body, a reputation, a legal right. Detrimental is broader and quieter: it describes anything that works against a thing's health or success, usually gradually. A fall is injurious the instant it happens; a habit is detrimental over months.

adverse: Adverse means working against you — adverse weather, an adverse ruling — conditions set unfavorably in your path. Detrimental goes further than opposition: it says real damage is being done. Adverse winds merely slow the ship; a detrimental leak steadily ruins the cargo.

damaging: Damaging means inflicting visible damage right now — a damaging storm, a damaging headline, harm you can point to at once. Detrimental emphasizes the slow, cumulative kind: it works against something's health or success over time. One damaging blow shows immediately; a detrimental habit shows up months later.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

beneficial: producing good or helpful results

advantageous: giving a useful edge or benefit

Where it sits · how serious and lasting the damage is

inconvenient → unfavorable → harmful → detrimental

inconvenient vs. detrimental: An inconvenient delay is a minor bother, but a detrimental one can genuinely damage the whole project.

unfavorable vs. detrimental: Unfavorable conditions merely work against you, while detrimental conditions actively cause real harm.

harmful vs. detrimental: Harmful covers any kind of damage, but detrimental emphasizes serious, lasting damage to something that matters, like a plan, relationship, or system.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — detriment: harm, damage, loss (from Latin deterere, 'to wear away') (Latin)

Suffix — -al: characteristic of; relating to (Latin (-alis))

Put it together: Detriment is an English word meaning harm, damage, or loss, and -al means 'characteristic of.' So detrimental describes anything characteristic of harm — something that damages a plan, relationship, or system.

Use the root in a new word: detriment: He kept gaming past midnight, to the detriment of his grades.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal

Use detrimental to describe something that causes lasting harm or damage, especially gradually or cumulatively. The key is that it's not just bad — it actively works against you. 'This habit is detrimental to your health' means the habit actively damages your health, not just that it's unhelpful.
